Defaming
dee-FAY-ming
n. / ppr. (the circulating of an evil report; the destruction of a man's name behind him)
From Latin diffamare, to spread abroad a report, from fama, rumour or reputation. In Jeremiah 20:10 it renders Hebrew dibbah, an evil report or slander — the same word used of the report the ten spies brought up on the land.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah has just been put in the stocks by Pashur the priest, and the lament that follows is the rawest passage in the book: For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side. Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting. The phrase fear on every side is the name Jeremiah had himself given to Pashur, thrown back at him now as a taunt. What breaks the prophet is not the stocks but the source of the whispering — all my familiars, the men of his own circle, watching not for his welfare but for his stumble, waiting with a report already half-written.

Paul knows the same weather from the apostolic side: Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day. The response in that verse is one word long and it is the whole Christian answer — we intreat, we entreat, we plead kindly. Not we retaliate, not we withdraw. And Jeremiah, in the very next breath after his complaint, turns and says the thing that holds a man up under it: But the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail. The defaming is real, the fear is real, and the one sentence that answers both is that the LORD is with him. Scripture does not promise the prophet a cleared name in his lifetime. It promises him the presence of God while the name is being taken.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): slandering; speaking evil of; injuring the reputation by false report.

expand to see more

DEFAME, v.t. To slander; falsely and maliciously to utter words respecting another which tend to injure his reputation or occupation.

DEFAMING, ppr. Slandering; injuring the good name and reputation.

DEFAMATION, n. The uttering of slanderous words with a view to injure another's reputation.

FAME, n. Public report or rumor; that which is said or reported abroad of a person.

OFFSCOURING, n. That which is scoured off; hence, refuse; recrement; any thing vile or despised.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 20:10 — "For I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side. Report, say they, and we will report it. All my familiars watched for my halting, saying, Peradventure he will be enticed, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him."

Jeremiah 20:11 — "But the LORD is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail: they shall be greatly ashamed; for they shall not prosper: their everlasting confusion shall never be forgotten."

1 Corinthians 4:13 — "Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day."

Psalm 31:13 — "For I have heard the slander of many: fear was on every side: while they took counsel together against me, they devised to take away my life."

Modern Corruption

Reputation is now destroyed at the speed of a network and restored at the speed of a court, and the gap between the two is where a great deal of modern cruelty lives.

expand to see more

Jeremiah's familiars needed a city gate and a few days. The machinery has changed and the sin has not: a report goes out, is repeated by men who have not checked it because repeating is cheap, and by the time anything is established the man is already what the report said he was. Report, say they, and we will report it is a perfect description of a feed. What Scripture supplies against it is not a technique but a standing: the LORD is with him as a mighty terrible one. That is the sentence Jeremiah reaches for in the same paragraph as his complaint, and it is the only thing that holds when a name cannot be cleared.

For the one tempted to join the reporting, the fence is older than any platform. Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness (Exodus 23:1) forbids not only the raising of the report but the lending of a hand to one already raised — and a forward, a repetition, a nod is a hand. The ninth commandment binds the repeater as it binds the originator, and Paul's one-word answer under defamation, we intreat, remains the pattern for a believer whose name is being taken: entreat, keep a good conscience, and leave the vindication with God, who forgets nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dibbah (H1681), an evil report or whispering; Greek dusphemeo (G1425), to speak ill of, rendered defamed.

expand to see more

Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — an evil report; the same noun used of the slander the spies brought up upon the land.

Greek dusphemeo (G1425) — to speak injuriously; used once, of the apostles in 1 Corinthians 4:13.

Hebrew magor missabib (H4036) — fear on every side; the name Jeremiah gave Pashur, returned to him as a taunt.

Hebrew tsela (H6761) — a halting, a limp; what the familiars watched for.

Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to entreat, to plead kindly; Paul's whole answer to being defamed.

Usage

"“I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side” — the prophet in the stocks."

"“Report, say they, and we will report it” — the machinery, unchanged."

"“Being defamed, we intreat” — the apostolic answer in two words."
